y1: During the grape harvest, it was necessary to harvest quickly before it rained, so there was a shortage of workers. The owner goes to the marketplace at 6 a.m., 9 a.m., 12 p.m., 3 p.m., and even at 5 p.m., one hour before sunset.
y2: Those standing at 5 p.m. said, “No one has hired us.” They were probably people who were not chosen because they were old or weak. The owner called them too.
y3: Usually, the worker looks for the owner, but this owner goes out to seek them himself five times. This is an image of God, like the Shepherd in chapter 9 and the shepherd seeking the lost sheep in chapter 18.
y5: The owner deliberately gave the wages starting from the last ones to arrive so everyone could see. When the one-hour worker received a denarius, the morning workers got their hopes up, but they also received one denarius. They grumbled, “You made them equal to us.”
y6: The owner's answer: “Friend, I am doing you no wrong. … Or is your evil eye envious because I am generous?” The morning worker lost nothing. The problem is a heart that cannot rejoice in the grace someone else receives.
y7: The morning worker in this parable is like the older brother of the prodigal son in Luke 15. A person who has been in the faith for a long time might envy the grace shown to a newcomer. This is also an answer to Peter's question in 19:27 (“What will we get?”).
y9: Jesus foretells His suffering for the third time and in the most detail: He will be handed over, condemned, mocked by the Gentiles, flogged, crucified, and raised on the third day. Right after this, the mother of Zebedee's sons asks for high places.
y10: Jesus asks: “Are you able to drink the cup that I am about to drink?” Then He says: “You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them. But it shall not be so among you. Whoever desires to become great among you shall be your servant.”
y11: A 'ransom' (lutron) is the price paid to free a slave or captive. Jesus came to give His life as this price. This is the fulfillment of the Suffering Servant in Isaiah 53. The peak of service is the cross.
y13: Jericho is the last gate on the road going up to Jerusalem. Two blind men by the road shouted, “Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David!” When the crowd rebuked them, they shouted even louder.
y14: Jesus asks: “What do you want me to do for you?” This is the same question He asked the mother in 20:21. The mother asked for power, while the blind men asked to see. Those whose eyes were opened followed Jesus. This was the road leading to the cross.
y15: The disciples who argued over positions even after hearing the prophecy of suffering three times, and the blind men who recognized Jesus as the 'Son of David' despite their physical blindness. Who is the one who truly sees?
verse: “Whoever desires to become great among you shall be your servant ... Even as the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.”
prayer: Jesus, who came to serve, I thank You for Your love in giving Your own life as the price for my life. Let me not envy the grace someone else receives, but rejoice together with them. Instead of asking for a high place, let my eyes be opened to see You, and let me follow You in the place of service. I pray in the name of Jesus Christ. Amen.
d0: denarius. It was enough money for a family to live on for one day. He gave even the one-hour worker 'enough to live for a day.' The owner met everyone's 'need'.
d1: evil eye. It is the 'bad eye' we learned about in 6:23. It is a heart that cannot rejoice in someone else's success. “Or is your evil eye envious because I am generous?” (20:15).
d2: cup. In the Old Testament, the 'cup of wrath' represents God's judgment. Jesus prays in Gethsemane, 'let this cup pass from me' (26:39). James later became the first martyr among the apostles (Acts 12:2).
d3: blind. Mark mentions only one by name (Bartimaeus), but Matthew says there were two. Two people were needed for a testimony (Deut. 19:15). In 9:27–31, two blind men also come with the same cry.
